title: Maple and the Sleepy Yawn
markdown:
In the gentle rolling Starberry Hills, where clouds played hide-and-seek with the sun, lived Maple, a little ogre with moss-green skin and honey-coloured eyes. Her mind buzzed like a happy bumblebee. Her home was a nook in a sunny hill, lined with moss and woven grasses, smelling of warm earth and sweet clover.

Marmie, her wonderfully fluffy marmot, had a pink nose that wiggled with curiosity and a talent for napping in sunbeams. Maple loved him dearly. She wanted to teach him a trick that would make them both smile.

Fetch, Marmie. Fetch the berry.

One warm morning, peach and rosy light on the hills, she placed a plump ruby-red berry near his dozing moss. “Today we will learn to fetch a berry.” Marmie wiggled his whiskers and snored like a tiny contented engine. Maple giggled, musical, and hugged him until his fluff tickled her chin.

“Fetch, Marmie! Fetch the berry, please!”

He sniffed, blinked, and flopped onto his back, paws up, asking for a tummy rub. She scratched. He sighed. Not quite.

Maybe brighter berries would help. She nestled him in a sling, fluffy head peeking, and ambled the dewy trail through feathery ferns and whispering trees. The air smelled of damp earth and flowers.

Elara, an elf messenger with moonlight wings, zipped past. “Hello, Maple! Off on an adventure?”

“I’m trying to teach Marmie to fetch berries. He mostly likes to nap and roll over.”

Elara hovered, kind. “Marmots. Sometimes the best tricks are the ones they learn themselves. Look for the brightest berry.” She chimed a laugh and left a shimmering trail. Maple did not need a lecture on patience. She had a sling full of marmot and a path still going.

In a peaceful hollow the sweetest blackberries grew, plump as dark jewels. Maple picked the largest, smelling of sunshine. “Now, Marmie. Fetch!” His nose twitched. A tiny paw nudged. Then he yawned, huge and sleepy. Maple’s heart wobbled. He was not fetching. He was getting very, very sleepy.

The sun dipped, long golden shadows. She picked up the berry. “I don’t think you’ll ever learn.” She leaned on a mossy rock. Marmie nudged her cheek, rumbling.

Then the peculiar thing: from her shoulder he yawned again, ambled back toward the nook, yawned, yawned, trailing sleepy yawns like a misty ribbon. He did not bring a berry. He was fetching yawns all the way home. A marmot trick, funny and his own.

Fetch, Marmie. Fetch the yawn.

She scooped him, warm, laughing. “That’s even better than berries.”

Moonlight painted the nook. They snuggled into blankets that felt like hugs. Marmie yawned a long slow whisper of sleep. Maple yawned too. The hills hushed. She held him close, safe and content, and they drifted, dreaming of sweet berries and the sleepiest trick in all the Starberry Hills.
audience: children aged 5-6, story time at home
author: StoryGen Community
